name: One
plain: In the Bible 'one' is less about counting and more about uniqueness and unity. Israel's central confession is that the LORD is one, and the New Testament uses 'one' for the union of Christ with the Father, of husband and wife, and of believers with each other.

meanings.note: The Shema (Deut 6:4) is Israel's basic creed. Jesus quotes it as the first commandment, and Paul restates it around Father and Lord Jesus in 1 Cor 8:6. Whether echad here means 'alone' (only God) or 'one' (undivided) is discussed; both senses fit.
'One flesh' describes a new kinship bond, not merely sexual union. Paul applies the same verse to Christ and the church.

meanings.meaning: Unity of the people of God
meanings.note: Jesus prays that his followers may be one as he and the Father are one; Paul lists 'one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God'.
The Greek uses the neuter hen ('one thing'), not the masculine 'one person'. Christians read this as unity of being or action; the precise sense is part of the later Trinitarian discussion.

otUsage: Used for God's singularity (Deut 6:4; Zech 14:9), for the united nation (Ezek 37:22 'one nation', the two sticks becoming one in Ezek 37:17), and for marriage (Gen 2:24).
ntUsage: Jesus quotes the Shema (Mark 12:29). John stresses the oneness of Father and Son (John 10:30) and prays for the disciples' unity (John 17:21). Paul builds his ethic of church unity on 'one' (Eph 4:4-6; 1 Cor 12:12-13).
caution: Most occurrences of 'one' are plain counting. Theological weight comes from context, not from the number itself.

name: Two
plain: Two is the number of a valid witness and of partnership. A charge needed two or three witnesses, Jesus sent his disciples out in pairs, and the covenant law was written on two tablets.

meanings.note: Israelite law required at least two witnesses. This shapes church discipline and possibly the 'two witnesses' of Revelation.
'Two are better than one.' The pairing of missionaries may also connect to the witness rule above.

meanings.meaning: The two tablets of the covenant
meanings.note: Later interpreters often split the commandments into duties to God and to neighbour, matching Jesus' two great commandments (Matt 22:37-40). The division of contents across the tablets is not stated; many scholars think each tablet was a full copy, as in ancient treaties.

Some popular numerology books (E. W. Bullinger, *Number in Scripture*) make two the number of division. The Bible does contrast two ways and two masters, but this is a feature of the teaching, not of the number.

otUsage: Animals entered the ark in pairs (Gen 7:9); two tablets of the law (Exod 31:18); two witnesses required (Deut 17:6; Deut 19:15); two cherubim over the ark (Exod 25:18).
ntUsage: Disciples sent in pairs (Mark 6:7); the witness rule in discipline (Matt 18:16; 1 Tim 5:19); two witnesses in Rev 11:3; the two great commandments (Matt 22:40).
caution: Pairs are often just pairs. Avoid turning every 'two' into a sign of division or witness.

name: Three
plain: Three often marks completeness or emphasis (holy, holy, holy) and is tied to the 'third day' as a day of decisive action, above all Jesus' resurrection. Christians later saw the Trinity in some threefold patterns, though the Bible never uses the number three to teach that doctrine.

meanings.meaning: The third day: turning point and deliverance
meanings.note: Abraham sees Moriah on the third day; God descends on Sinai on the third day. Paul says Christ was raised on the third day 'according to the scriptures', and Hos 6:2 and Jonah are the passages most often proposed as what he had in mind.
Hebrew can emphasise by repeating a word; the triple 'holy' is the strongest such case. The priestly blessing has three lines.

meanings.meaning: Threefold denial and restoration of Peter
meanings.note: Peter denies Jesus three times and is asked 'do you love me?' three times. Most readers see a deliberate match in John.

The baptismal formula and Paul's blessing name Father, Son and Spirit together. Church Fathers also saw the Trinity in the three visitors to Abraham and in the triple 'holy'. The New Testament texts are explicit about the three names; the OT readings are tradition, not the plain sense.

otUsage: Third-day events (Gen 22:4; Exod 19:11; Esth 5:1), three annual pilgrim feasts (Exod 23:14), a threefold cord (Eccl 4:12), three days of Jonah in the fish (Jonah 1:17).
ntUsage: Resurrection on the third day (Luke 24:46; 1 Cor 15:4); three disciples close to Jesus (Mark 9:2); three temptations (Matt 4:1-11); faith, hope and love (1 Cor 13:13); three prayers in Gethsemane (Matt 26:44).
caution: 'Three days' in Hebrew idiom can mean parts of three days, which is why Friday-to-Sunday can be 'three days and three nights' (Matt 12:40). Reading every triad as Trinitarian goes beyond the text.

name: Four
plain: Four is the number of the whole earth: four winds, four corners, four directions. Visionary books use it for things that cover the world, such as four kingdoms, four horsemen and four living creatures.

meanings.meaning: The whole world in every direction
meanings.note: 'Four corners' and 'four winds' were ordinary ways of saying 'everywhere', not a claim that the earth is square.

meanings.meaning: The living creatures around God's throne
meanings.note: Four creatures with faces of man, lion, ox and eagle represent all creation (or all living beings) serving God. Irenaeus assigned them to the four Gospels (*Against Heresies* 3.11.8); the pairing of which creature goes with which Gospel varied among later writers.
Four metals and four beasts stand for four kingdoms that rule the known world before God's kingdom comes. Which four is debated (see 'beast').
Four horsemen echo Zechariah's four chariots and Ezekiel's four 'sore judgements' (sword, famine, wild beasts, pestilence).

otUsage: Four rivers from Eden (Gen 2:10), four creatures in Ezekiel (Ezek 1:5), four kingdoms in Daniel (Dan 7:3), four chariots and horns in Zechariah (Zech 1:18; Zech 6:1).
ntUsage: Gathering the elect from the four winds (Matt 24:31; Mark 13:27); four living creatures (Rev 4:6); four angels at the four corners (Rev 7:1); four horsemen (Rev 6:1-8).
caution: Four is mostly symbolic in apocalyptic visions. In narrative (four days Lazarus was dead, John 11:39) it is usually just a fact, though John may stress it to show Lazarus was truly dead.

name: Five
plain: Five has no strong, agreed symbolic meaning in the Bible. It appears in memorable places (five loaves, five smooth stones, five wise and five foolish virgins), and Jewish tradition counts five books of Moses, but claims that five means 'grace' come from modern numerology rather than the text.

meanings.meaning: A small, ordinary amount used by God
meanings.note: David's five stones and the five loaves stress smallness. Paul would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in a tongue.

meanings.meaning: The five books of the Law
meanings.note: The Torah (Pentateuch) is five books. The Bible does not count them itself; the fivefold division is old Jewish tradition. Some scholars think Matthew arranges Jesus' teaching in five great speeches as a new Torah (Matt 7:28; Matt 11:1; Matt 13:53; Matt 19:1; Matt 26:1 mark their endings), which is a popular but debated reading.
Restitution for wrongs added a fifth (20 percent). This is a legal amount, not a symbol.
E. W. Bullinger and later popular writers called five the number of grace. There is no text that makes this link; treat it as speculation.

otUsage: Five stones (1 Sam 17:40), the restitution fifth (Lev 6:5), five cities of Egypt speaking Canaan's language (Isa 19:18), five kings in a cave (Josh 10:16).
ntUsage: Five loaves (Mark 6:38), five wise and five foolish virgins (Matt 25:2), the Samaritan woman's five husbands (John 4:18), five porches at Bethesda (John 5:2).
caution: Some read the Samaritan woman's five husbands as Samaria's five imported gods (2 Kgs 17:24-31). This is an old allegorical idea and remains speculative. Most fives are simply counts.

name: Six
plain: Six is the number of the days of work, and humans were made on the sixth day. Because it falls one short of seven, many interpreters see it as the number of what is human or incomplete, which helps explain 666 in Revelation. That reading is widely held but not stated in the text.

meanings.note: Six days of work lead to sabbath; a Hebrew slave served six years and went free in the seventh.

meanings.meaning: Humanity, especially humanity apart from God
meanings.note: Revelation calls 666 'the number of a man' (or 'a human number'). Some take six as falling short of seven, the number of completion; others say the phrase simply means humans can calculate it.
Goliath is six cubits and a span; Nebuchadnezzar's image is sixty by six cubits. Some see a pattern of proud human power; others say these are just measurements.

otUsage: Six days of creation and work (Gen 1:31; Exod 20:9), six years of servitude (Exod 21:2), six cities of refuge (Num 35:6), six steps to Solomon's throne (1 Kgs 10:19).
ntUsage: Six stone water jars at Cana (John 2:6), 'six days before the Passover' (John 12:1), the sixth hour of darkness (Mark 15:33), and 666 (Rev 13:18).
caution: Six jars at Cana are often preached as 'imperfect Judaism awaiting Christ'. That may be John's hint, but it is not stated. Do not build doctrine on it.

name: Seven
plain: Seven is the Bible's best-known symbolic number. Rooted in the seven-day week that ends in God's rest, it signals completeness, fullness and something God has set apart. Revelation is built on sevens. But many sevens in the Bible are just counts.

meanings.note: The seventh day crowns creation and becomes Israel's sabbath. Hebrews treats God's rest as a promise still open to believers.

meanings.meaning: Holiness and covenant (sabbath years, jubilee, oaths)
meanings.note: Sabbath years, the jubilee after seven sevens, blood sprinkled seven times. The Hebrew verb 'to swear an oath' (shava) is built on the same root as seven, and Beersheba is called 'well of the oath' or 'well of seven' with seven lambs as witness (Gen 21:28-31).
'Seven times more' means fully. Jericho is circled seven times on the seventh day; Naaman washes seven times.

Seven churches, seals, trumpets, bowls; seven spirits; the Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes. Seven churches are real congregations that also stand for the whole church. The 'seven spirits' are read as the Holy Spirit in fullness (Isa 11:2 is often cited) or as seven angels; this is debated.
Peter offers seven as generous; Jesus multiplies it beyond counting. See 'seventy times seven'.

otUsage: Creation week (Gen 2:2), clean animals by sevens (Gen 7:2), Pharaoh's seven years of plenty and famine (Gen 41:26-30), the sevenfold lampstand (Exod 25:37), Jericho (Josh 6:4), seven pillars of wisdom (Prov 9:1), seven eyes on the stone (Zech 3:9).
ntUsage: Seven loaves and seven baskets (Mark 8:5-8), seven demons from Mary Magdalene (Luke 8:2), seven deacons (Acts 6:3), and the many sevens of Revelation (Rev 1:20; Rev 5:1; Rev 8:2; Rev 16:1).
caution: Not every seven is symbolic. The seven men of Acts 6:3 or seven sons of Sceva (Acts 19:14) may simply be how many there were. Count-the-sevens arguments (for example claims of hidden seven-patterns in the Greek text) are speculative and easy to manufacture.

name: Eight
plain: Eight comes after a complete week, so it can suggest a new start. Circumcision happened on the eighth day, eight people came through the flood, and early Christians called Sunday, the day of the resurrection, 'the eighth day'.

meanings.note: Boys were circumcised on the eighth day; Jesus and Paul both were.

meanings.meaning: A new beginning after the flood
meanings.note: Peter notes that eight souls were saved through water and links this to baptism. Whether he means eight as symbolic or just accurate is not said.

meanings.meaning: The eighth day as resurrection and new creation
meanings.note: The Feast of Tabernacles ended with an eighth-day assembly. The *Epistle of Barnabas* (15.9) and Justin Martyr (*Dialogue with Trypho* 41) call Sunday the eighth day, the day of resurrection and new world. This is early church tradition, not a biblical statement.

In Greek letters-as-numbers the name Iesous adds to 888, and some ancient writers (the Christian parts of the *Sibylline Oracles*) noted this as a contrast with 666. This is gematria (see 666) and is speculative as an interpretation of Scripture.

otUsage: Circumcision (Gen 17:12), consecration of priests completed on the eighth day (Lev 9:1), the eighth-day assembly of Tabernacles (Lev 23:36), David as Jesse's eighth son (1 Sam 17:12).
ntUsage: Jesus circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21); 'after eight days' Jesus appears to Thomas (John 20:26); eight saved in the ark (1 Pet 3:20); the beast that is 'an eighth' king (Rev 17:11).
caution: The resurrection 'on the eighth day' idea is a lovely early Christian reflection, but the New Testament itself says 'the first day of the week' (Mark 16:2).

name: Ten
plain: Ten is a round, complete number for counting, like fingers on two hands. The Ten Commandments, ten plagues and the tithe (a tenth) make it important, but its symbolism is mostly 'a full set'.

meanings.note: The Hebrew calls them 'the ten words'. Jews, Catholics/Lutherans and Reformed/Orthodox number them differently, though all count ten.
The tithe gives back a tenth. Whether Christians are bound to tithe is debated; the NT stresses generous giving (2 Cor 9:7).

meanings.meaning: Full measure of judgement or testing
meanings.note: Ten plagues; Israel tested God 'ten times'; ten days of testing in Daniel and Smyrna. In some cases ten seems to mean 'many' or 'a limited, set period'.

meanings.meaning: Ten horns as a confederation of rulers
meanings.note: Explained in the text as ten kings. Identifying them with particular modern nations (for example a ten-nation Europe) is speculative.

otUsage: Ten commandments (Exod 34:28), ten plagues (Exod 7:14-12:30), Abraham bargaining down to ten righteous (Gen 18:32), ten times better (Dan 1:20).
ntUsage: Ten virgins (Matt 25:1), ten lepers (Luke 17:12), ten minas (Luke 19:13), ten days of tribulation (Rev 2:10), ten horns (Rev 12:3).
caution: Jewish tradition later made ten men the minimum for public prayer (the minyan), partly from Gen 18:32. That is tradition, not a biblical rule.

name: Twelve
plain: Twelve is the number of God's people: twelve sons of Jacob became the twelve tribes of Israel, and Jesus chose twelve apostles, signalling the renewal of Israel. In Revelation the new Jerusalem is built on twelves.

meanings.note: Twelve sons, twelve tribes, twelve pillars and twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate. The list of tribes varies (Levi in or out, Joseph as one or as Ephraim and Manasseh), but the total is kept at twelve.

meanings.meaning: The renewed Israel gathered by Jesus
meanings.note: Jesus' choice of twelve is widely read by historians as a deliberate sign of restoring Israel. The apostles replace Judas to keep the number at twelve.

meanings.meaning: The complete people of God, old and new together
meanings.note: The new Jerusalem has twelve gates named for the tribes and twelve foundations named for the apostles. Many see the whole people of God across both covenants.

Jesus asks the disciples to notice the numbers twelve and seven at the feedings. Many read twelve as Israel's abundance and seven (Mark 8:8) as fullness for the Gentiles; this is a common but debated reading.

otUsage: Twelve tribes (Gen 49:28), twelve spies (Num 13:2), twelve stones from the Jordan (Josh 4:3), twelve oxen under the bronze sea (1 Kgs 7:25), twelve stones of Elijah's altar (1 Kgs 18:31).
ntUsage: Twelve apostles (Matt 10:1-4), a twelve-year illness and a twelve-year-old girl (Mark 5:25; Mark 5:42), twelve legions of angels (Matt 26:53), twelves throughout the new Jerusalem (Rev 21:12-21).
caution: In Mark 5 the two twelves link the stories, but they are also real ages and durations. Symbolism and history are not opposites here.

name: Forty
plain: Forty is the Bible's number for a period of testing, waiting or preparation, often ending in a new start. It also works as a round number for a generation.

meanings.note: Israel's forty years in the wilderness, Elijah's forty days to Horeb, and Jesus' forty days of fasting form a deliberate chain; Jesus succeeds where Israel failed (he answers the devil from Deuteronomy).
Forty days of flood rain; forty days for Nineveh to repent.
Moses forty days on the mountain; the risen Jesus appears over forty days.

meanings.meaning: A round number for a generation
meanings.note: Forty-year periods (rest under judges, reigns of David and Solomon) and the 480 years of 1 Kgs 6:1 (12 x 40) are widely taken as partly schematic. This matters for dating the exodus (early vs late date).

otUsage: Flood (Gen 7:12), Moses' life in three forties (Acts 7:23; Acts 7:30; Deut 34:7), wilderness years (Num 14:34), spies' forty days (Num 13:25), Goliath's forty days of taunting (1 Sam 17:16), Elijah (1 Kgs 19:8).
ntUsage: Jesus' fast (Matt 4:2), the post-resurrection appearances (Acts 1:3), forty lashes minus one (2 Cor 11:24; Deut 25:3).
caution: The Church's Lent of forty days is a later tradition built on these passages. Not every forty is symbolic, and round numbers do not mean events did not happen.

name: Fifty
plain: Fifty marks the year of jubilee (after seven sevens of years) and the feast fifty days after Passover, which Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost. It carries ideas of release, harvest and fulfilment.

meanings.note: In the fiftieth year land returned to families and slaves went free. Jesus' sermon at Nazareth uses jubilee language. Whether Israel ever fully kept the jubilee is debated by historians.

meanings.meaning: Pentecost: harvest and the gift of the Spirit
meanings.note: Fifty days after the Passover sheaf came the Feast of Weeks. The Spirit is poured out on that day. Later Jewish tradition tied the feast to the giving of the Law at Sinai; that link is tradition, and its date is debated.
Captains of fifty, crowds seated in fifties. Mostly practical.

otUsage: Jubilee (Lev 25:10), Pentecost count (Lev 23:16), Abraham's plea for fifty righteous (Gen 18:24), Levites serving until age fifty (Num 4:3; Num 8:25), Obadiah hiding prophets by fifty (1 Kgs 18:4).
ntUsage: Pentecost (Acts 2:1; Acts 20:16; 1 Cor 16:8), crowds in fifties (Luke 9:14), 'You are not yet fifty years old' (John 8:57).
caution: Calculations that use jubilee cycles to date the end of the world are speculative and have repeatedly failed.

name: Seventy
plain: Seventy (ten times seven) suggests a full company or a full span. Seventy descendants of Jacob went to Egypt, seventy elders helped Moses, the exile lasted 'seventy years', and Jesus sent out seventy (or seventy-two) disciples.

meanings.meaning: The full family of Israel and of the nations
meanings.note: Jacob's household numbered seventy. Genesis 10 lists about seventy nations (the Hebrew and Greek texts count slightly differently), and Jewish tradition spoke of seventy nations of the world.
Seventy elders share Moses' burden and receive the Spirit. Later Jewish tradition modelled the Sanhedrin (about seventy-one members) on this; that is tradition.
Scholars debate whether seventy is exact (605 to 536 BC, or 586 to 516 BC both give about seventy) or a round 'lifetime' figure (Ps 90:10).

Seventy 'sevens' are given for Israel's restoration. Readings include: fulfilled in Christ's ministry and death; fulfilled under Antiochus IV in the 160s BC (most critical scholars); a gap before the seventieth week (dispensationalists). See 'three-and-a-half'.
Manuscripts are split between seventy and seventy-two (as with the nations in Gen 10). Many think Luke signals a mission reaching all nations, matching the count in Genesis 10.

otUsage: Jacob's family (Gen 46:27), the seventy elders (Num 11:16), seventy palm trees at Elim (Exod 15:27), seventy sons of Gideon and Ahab (Judg 8:30; 2 Kgs 10:1), a lifetime of 'threescore years and ten' (Ps 90:10).
ntUsage: The seventy (or seventy-two) sent out (Luke 10:1); forgiveness 'seventy times seven' (Matt 18:22).
caution: The Greek Old Testament is called the Septuagint ('seventy') from a legend of seventy-two translators in the *Letter of Aristeas*. That is a tradition with legendary features, not history in every detail.

name: Seventy times seven
plain: When Peter asks if he should forgive seven times, Jesus says 'seventy times seven' (or 'seventy-seven times'). Either way the point is the same: forgiveness should not be counted. The phrase reverses Lamech's boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge.

meanings.note: The parable that follows (the unforgiving servant) shows why: those forgiven a huge debt must forgive. The number is not a quota of 490.
The Greek Old Testament uses the same expression for Lamech's 'seventy-sevenfold' revenge. Most commentators see Jesus deliberately reversing it.
The Greek can mean 77 or 70 x 7. The Gen 4:24 parallel favours 77 (most modern versions), while KJV and older readers took 490. The sense does not change.

meanings.meaning: A link to Daniel's seventy sevens
meanings.note: Some preachers connect 490 to Daniel's seventy weeks as a 'jubilee of forgiveness'. This is an interesting echo but speculative.

otUsage: Lamech's song of revenge (Gen 4:24).
ntUsage: Jesus' answer to Peter (Matt 18:22); the parallel in Luke speaks of forgiving seven times a day (Luke 17:4).
caution: Forgiveness without limit is not the same as ignoring harm or abandoning accountability; the same chapter gives steps for confronting sin (Matt 18:15-17).

plain: Revelation hears the number of the sealed servants of God: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes. Christians disagree whether this is a literal group of Jewish believers, a symbol for the whole church, or a special class. The number is 12 x 12 x 1,000, which suggests symbolism to many readers.

meanings.meaning: The whole people of God, pictured as a complete army of Israel
meanings.note: John hears a number, then turns and sees an uncountable multitude from every nation, just as he hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb (Rev 5:5-6). On this reading, the 144,000 and the multitude are the same people seen two ways. Held by many Reformed, Catholic and amillennial scholars (e.g. G. K. Beale, Richard Bauckham).

meanings.meaning: A literal group of Jewish believers
meanings.note: Dispensational interpreters take the tribes literally: 144,000 Jewish believers sealed during a future tribulation, distinct from the Gentile multitude.

meanings.meaning: A Christian elite or martyr group
meanings.note: Some see them as martyrs or especially faithful believers ('firstfruits'). Jehovah's Witnesses teach that 144,000 'anointed' will rule in heaven while others live on earth, a view other Christian groups reject.

otUsage: Builds on the twelve tribes and on military census lists (Num 1:2-3; Num 31:4-5).
ntUsage: Only in Revelation (Rev 7:4; Rev 14:1-3). Note the unusual tribe list: Judah first, Dan missing, both Joseph and Manasseh named (Rev 7:5-8), which many think shows it is a stylised list.
caution: The wall of the new Jerusalem is 144 cubits and the city 12,000 stadia (Rev 21:16-17); Revelation clearly enjoys multiples of twelve. Be careful about building a two-class church on a single number.

plain: Revelation says the beast's number is 666, 'the number of a man', and invites the wise to calculate it. In the ancient world letters doubled as numbers (gematria), so a name could add up to a number. The most popular scholarly answer is the emperor Nero, but other readings are held, and modern attempts to name a living person have a long record of failure.

meanings.note: 'Nero Caesar' spelled in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr) adds to 666; spelled from the Latin form without the final n it adds to 616, the variant known to Irenaeus and found in an early papyrus (P115). Many scholars think this explains the variant. Critics note the Hebrew spelling must be chosen, and Revelation's readers spoke Greek.

meanings.meaning: A symbol of falling short, three times over
meanings.note: Six is one less than seven; triple six may parody the threefold holiness of God, a counterfeit trinity (dragon, beast, false prophet, Rev 16:13). Popular among idealist readers. Possible, but the text says 'calculate', which suggests a specific name.
Futurist readers expect a person whose name will fit. Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 5.30) already warned against confident guessing and offered only cautious suggestions.
Solomon received 666 talents of gold a year just before his fall into idolatry and excess. Some see the beast as power and wealth turned against God. A suggestive parallel, but not proven.

otUsage: Solomon's yearly gold (1 Kgs 10:14); the 666 sons of Adonikam (Ezra 2:13), which is just a census figure.
ntUsage: Only Rev 13:18. The mark on hand or forehead (Rev 13:16-17) contrasts with God's seal on the foreheads of his servants (Rev 7:3; Rev 14:1) and echoes Deut 6:8, so it is about loyalty and worship, not only a physical mark.
caution: Gematria can make almost any name add to 666 with enough adjustments; popes, emperors, dictators and presidents have all been 'identified'. Treat any precise modern identification as speculative.

name: One thousand
plain: A thousand often means 'very many' or 'a vast span'. Its most debated use is the thousand years of Revelation 20, the 'millennium'. Christians read it as a future literal reign, as the present age of the church, or as a coming golden age before Christ returns.

meanings.note: Cattle on a thousand hills; love to a thousand generations. Clearly not counts.
Peter uses this to explain the apparent delay of Christ's return. It is not a formula for 'one day = 1,000 years'.

meanings.meaning: The millennium as a future literal reign (premillennial)
meanings.note: Christ returns and then reigns for a thousand years on earth before the final judgement. Held by many early Fathers (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus) and by modern premillennialists.

meanings.meaning: The millennium as the present church age (amillennial)
meanings.note: Satan is bound now (Jesus binds the strong man), and the saints reign with Christ now. Influential through Augustine (*City of God* 20.7-9) and held by many Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Reformed.

meanings.meaning: A golden age before Christ returns (postmillennial)
meanings.note: The gospel gradually transforms the world, then Christ returns. Strong among Puritans and 19th-century evangelicals; held today by some Reformed writers.

otUsage: Thousands as large numbers (Exod 20:6; Ps 50:10; Ps 90:4); military units of a thousand (Num 31:4).
ntUsage: 2 Pet 3:8 and Rev 20:2-7, where 'thousand years' appears six times.
caution: Revelation's numbers are often symbolic (seven horns, twelve thousand per tribe), which supports but does not prove a symbolic thousand. Each millennial view has able defenders; see the debate page.

name: Three and a half (42 months, 1,260 days)
original: Aramaic iddan ve-iddanin u-pelag iddan; Greek kairon kai kairous kai hēmisu kairou
plain: Daniel and Revelation speak of a limited time of trouble in several ways: 'a time, times and half a time', 42 months, and 1,260 days. All equal about three and a half years, half of seven. The idea is a period of real suffering that God has cut short. Readers disagree whether it is a literal future period, a past one, or a symbol for the whole church age.

meanings.meaning: A broken, limited time of persecution
meanings.note: Half of seven: the enemy's time is real but cut off. This basic meaning is shared across views.

Most critical scholars read Daniel's half-week as the roughly three years when the temple was desecrated (167-164 BC). Many conservative scholars see Daniel looking further ahead as well, or primarily.
Futurists, especially dispensationalists, see the second half of a seven-year tribulation before Christ returns.

meanings.meaning: The church age between Christ's ascension and return
meanings.note: Idealist and many amillennial readers note the woman flees to the wilderness after the child is taken up to God, so the 1,260 days cover the church's whole wilderness journey.

Historicists (e.g. many Reformers and later Adventists) took each day as a year and dated 1,260 years of papal power. This depends on a debated principle and is little held today outside some traditions.

otUsage: Daniel's 'time, times and half a time' (Dan 7:25; Dan 12:7) and the half week (Dan 9:27). The 1,290 and 1,335 days (Dan 12:11-12) are unexplained extensions.
ntUsage: Revelation uses all three forms (Rev 11:2-3; Rev 12:6; Rev 12:14; Rev 13:5). Jesus and James say Elijah's drought lasted three years and six months (Luke 4:25; Jas 5:17), while 1 Kgs 18:1 says rain came 'in the third year', perhaps counting from a different point.
caution: Date-setting from these numbers has a long record of failed predictions. Note that Revelation uses three different forms for the same span, which suggests the length is symbolic.

name: 153 fish
plain: After the resurrection the disciples catch 153 large fish and the net does not tear. John gives the exact number, which has puzzled readers for centuries. It may be an eyewitness memory, a symbol of the whole world's harvest, or a mathematical puzzle; no reading has won general agreement.

meanings.note: Fishermen count and share catches. John stresses eyewitness testimony in the same chapter. Many commentators think this is the simplest explanation, possibly alongside symbolism.

meanings.meaning: All nations gathered: every kind of fish
meanings.note: Jerome (*Commentary on Ezekiel*, on Ezek 47) says ancient naturalists counted 153 species of fish, so the catch stands for all peoples. The claim about the naturalist (Oppian) does not match surviving texts, so the source is doubtful.

meanings.meaning: A triangular number: the sum of 1 to 17
meanings.note: Augustine (*Tractates on John* 122.8) notes 153 is 1+2+...+17 and reads 17 as 10 (Law) plus 7 (Spirit). Mathematically true; the meaning he attaches is tradition.

Ezekiel's river from the temple fills the Dead Sea with fish 'from En-gedi to En-eglaim'. J. A. Emerton (1958) proposed that these names produce 17 and 153 by letter-values. Ingenious but speculative.

otUsage: No OT occurrence; Ezekiel's vision of fishermen (Ezek 47:10) is the most-cited background.
ntUsage: Only John 21:11. Contrast the earlier miraculous catch where the nets begin to break (Luke 5:6).
caution: When a number has had many clever explanations and none prevails, hold all of them lightly. The clear point of the scene is the abundant catch at Jesus' word and the net that holds.

plain: Abraham rescues Lot with 318 trained men. An early Christian writing, the *Epistle of Barnabas*, read 318 in Greek letters as a hidden picture of Jesus and the cross. This is a famous example of ancient gematria, not the plain sense of Genesis.

meanings.note: The plain sense: Abraham's armed servants, born in his household. The number is unusual and specific, which suggests an old record rather than a symbol.

*Barnabas* 9.7-9 notes that in Greek numerals 318 is T (300) plus I and H (18). IH are the first letters of Iesous, and T is shaped like the cross. Note this uses Greek letters, which Abraham did not use, and Barnabas treats circumcision of 318 as the point (combining Gen 14 with Gen 17).
Some rabbinic sources note that the Hebrew letters of Eliezer, Abraham's servant, add to 318, suggesting Abraham went with Eliezer alone. Tradition, and plainly not the narrative's meaning.

Later church tradition gave the number of bishops at the Council of Nicaea (325) as 318 and some writers linked it to Abraham. The actual attendance is uncertain (ancient estimates range from about 250 to 318).

otUsage: Only Gen 14:14.
ntUsage: None. The NT does not interpret this number; Hebrews mentions the battle only in passing (Heb 7:1).
caution: Barnabas shows how early Christians sometimes read the Old Testament: by clever wordplay that the original authors could not have meant. Valuable as history of interpretation; not a model for exegesis.

name: White
plain: White in the Bible stands for purity, victory and the glory of God. Sins are washed 'white as snow', the transfigured Jesus shines white, and the redeemed in Revelation wear white robes washed in the Lamb's blood.

meanings.note: The paradox of Rev 7:14 (robes made white in blood) shows white is about forgiveness through sacrifice, not natural innocence.
The Ancient of Days has white clothing and hair; Jesus' clothes shine at the transfiguration; the final judgement is from a great white throne.

meanings.meaning: Victory and righteousness of the saints
meanings.note: Revelation explains the bride's fine linen as 'the righteous deeds of the saints'. White robes are also festal and victory clothing in the Greco-Roman world.
Angels at the tomb and ascension appear in white or shining clothes.

otUsage: Snow and wool as images of cleansing (Isa 1:18), white garments for joy (Eccl 9:8), white hair of the Ancient of Days (Dan 7:9). In skin-disease laws, white hair or patches could be a sign of uncleanness (Lev 13:3), so white is not always positive.
ntUsage: Transfiguration (Mark 9:3), angels (Matt 28:3), and many uses in Revelation: white robes, white horse, white stone with a new name (Rev 2:17), white cloud (Rev 14:14), white throne (Rev 20:11).
caution: Biblical white imagery is about light and cleanness, not skin colour. Using it to rank human races is a misuse with an ugly history.

name: Red and scarlet
original: Hebrew adom, shani (tolaat shani, 'scarlet worm'); Greek kokkinos, pyrros
plain: Red is the colour of blood, so it carries both life and violence. Scarlet thread or wool appears in cleansing rituals and in Rahab's rescue, while red and scarlet also mark the bloodshed of war and the luxury of Babylon in Revelation.

meanings.note: 'Though your sins be as scarlet.' Scarlet dye was colourfast, so the image is of a stain that will not wash out, except by God.
Scarlet wool with cedar and hyssop was used in purification; the red heifer's ashes cleansed from death. Hebrews gathers these into Christ's work.

Rahab's scarlet cord marks her house for safety. Christian writers from Clement of Rome (*1 Clement* 12) onward saw it as a sign of redemption through blood, recalling the Passover blood on doorposts. Tradition, not the stated meaning.
The red horse takes peace from the earth; the warrior's garments are red as one who treads the winepress.
Babylon rides a scarlet beast and wears purple and scarlet. Soldiers mock Jesus with a scarlet (Matthew) or purple (Mark, John) cloak, parodying royalty.

otUsage: Scarlet thread on Zerah's hand (Gen 38:28), tabernacle curtains of scarlet yarn (Exod 26:1), purification (Lev 14:4), Esau/Edom the 'red' one (Gen 25:30), a wife clothing her household in scarlet (Prov 31:21).
ntUsage: Scarlet robe at the mocking (Matt 27:28), red horse and red dragon (Rev 6:4; Rev 12:3), scarlet beast and woman (Rev 17:3-4), scarlet wool in Hebrews (Heb 9:19).
caution: A popular sermon links Ps 22:6 ('I am a worm', Hebrew tolaat) to the scarlet-dye insect to picture Christ's blood. The word tolaat is the general word for worm; the connection is speculative.

name: Purple
plain: Purple dye, made from sea snails, was very expensive, so purple meant royalty, wealth and high status. It was woven into the tabernacle and priestly clothes, worn by kings, mocked onto Jesus, and sold by Lydia.

meanings.note: Kings of Midian wore purple; Mordecai and Daniel are honoured with it.

meanings.meaning: Holiness and beauty of God's dwelling
meanings.note: Blue, purple and scarlet yarn are the standard trio for the tabernacle and priestly garments.
The irony is that the mocked king is the true king.

meanings.meaning: Wealth that ignores God and neighbour
meanings.note: The rich man in purple ignores Lazarus; Babylon trades in purple.

otUsage: Tabernacle fabric (Exod 26:1), priestly garments (Exod 28:5), royal dress (Judg 8:26), the capable wife's clothing (Prov 31:22), the lover's hair 'like purple' (Song 7:5).
ntUsage: Jesus' mocking robe (Mark 15:17), the rich man (Luke 16:19), Lydia the seller of purple (Acts 16:14), Babylon (Rev 17:4; Rev 18:16).
caution: Purple itself is neutral; it signals status. Whether that status is honoured or condemned depends on the story.

name: Blue (tekhelet)
plain: The Hebrew tekhelet was a costly blue-violet dye. Israelites wore a blue cord on the tassels of their garments to remember God's commands, and the high priest wore a robe all of blue. Jewish tradition linked the colour to sea, sky and God's throne.

meanings.note: The blue thread in the tassels was a visible reminder to obey and not follow one's own heart.
The high priest's robe was all blue; blue cloths covered the holiest furnishings when moved.

meanings.meaning: Heaven and the throne of God
meanings.note: Under God's feet was a sapphire pavement 'like the very heaven'. The Talmud (*Menachot* 43b) says tekhelet resembles the sea, the sea the sky, and the sky the throne of glory. That chain is tradition.

otUsage: Tabernacle and priestly fabric (Exod 26:1; Exod 28:31), tassels (Num 15:38), Persian palace hangings (Esth 1:6).
ntUsage: Almost absent as a symbol. Jacinth (hyacinth-blue) appears in breastplates of the demonic cavalry (Rev 9:17) and as a foundation stone (Rev 21:20). Jesus' tassels (Matt 9:20; Matt 14:36) would have had tekhelet if dye was available.
caution: The exact shade and source of tekhelet are debated (most scholars favour a sea snail, Murex trunculus). Ancient colour words do not match modern categories well.

name: Black
plain: Black in the Bible is mostly linked to mourning, famine, judgement and darkness. It is not used to describe a people as evil; in Song of Songs the woman is 'black and beautiful'.

meanings.note: The black horse carries scales and food prices that mean famine.
Heavens darken and the sun becomes black as sackcloth (dark goat-hair cloth worn in mourning).
'Blackness of darkness' (KJV) describes the fate of false teachers.

meanings.meaning: Simple description of beauty or health
meanings.note: The woman is sun-darkened and beautiful; the beloved's hair is black as a raven; black hair can show healing.

otUsage: Darkened skin from suffering (Job 30:30; Lam 4:8), darkened heavens (Jer 4:28), horses in Zechariah's vision (Zech 6:2; Zech 6:6), sunburnt beauty (Song 1:5).
ntUsage: Hair black or white (Matt 5:36), the black horse (Rev 6:5), the black sun (Rev 6:12), blackness of darkness (Jude 1:13).
caution: The so-called 'curse of Ham' used to justify racial slavery misreads Gen 9:25: the curse falls on Canaan, and nothing is said about skin colour. Biblical darkness imagery is about light and its absence, not ethnicity.

name: Green
plain: Green is the colour of life, growth and God's provision: green pastures, green leaves of the righteous. Because pagan shrines were often under leafy trees, 'under every green tree' became a phrase for idolatry.

meanings.note: God gives green plants for food; the shepherd leads to green pastures. Mark notes the green grass at the feeding, perhaps an eyewitness touch of springtime.
Trees that stay green in drought picture those who trust God.
Hill-top shrines and sacred trees; 'under every green tree' became a formula.
'If they do this when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?' Most read it as: if the innocent Jesus suffers so, how much worse for guilty Jerusalem. Exact sense debated.

otUsage: Green plants for food (Gen 1:30), green pastures (Ps 23:2), the wicked flourishing like a green tree only for a time (Ps 37:35), idolatrous groves (Deut 12:2).
ntUsage: Green grass (Mark 6:39; Rev 8:7; Rev 9:4), green and dry wood (Luke 23:31). The same Greek word chlōros is the 'pale' horse of Rev 6:8.
caution: Green is not a liturgical or mystical code in Scripture; church calendars using green for 'ordinary time' are later tradition.

name: Gold (as colour and splendour)
plain: Gold stands for the highest value, royal splendour and the glory of God's presence. The holiest objects in the tabernacle and temple were gold, and the new Jerusalem is pure gold like clear glass. Gold can also become an idol, as with the golden calf.

meanings.note: The ark, lampstand and inner temple were gold. The whole new city is gold, as though the holy of holies now fills everything (it is also cube-shaped, Rev 21:16, like the holy of holies in 1 Kgs 6:20).

The head of gold is Babylon; the magi bring gold to a king; elders wear golden crowns. Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 3.9.2) and later Fathers read the gold as a sign of kingship, incense of deity and myrrh of death; tradition.
Gold is purified by fire; faith tested by trials is more precious.
The golden calf and Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue; hoarded gold that corrodes.

otUsage: Tabernacle furnishings (Exod 25), Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 6:22), wisdom better than gold (Prov 8:19), God's words sweeter and more desirable than gold (Ps 19:10), 'the gold is mine' (Hag 2:8).
ntUsage: Magi's gift (Matt 2:11), tested faith (1 Pet 1:7), golden lampstands and sash (Rev 1:12-13), golden bowls of incense as prayers (Rev 5:8), the golden city (Rev 21:18).
caution: Gold as a metal and precious stone is covered separately under metals and stones. Prosperity readings that treat gold streets as a promise of present wealth misread the vision.

name: Pale (the pale horse)
plain: The fourth horse in Revelation is chlōros, the same word used for green grass. Here it means the sickly grey-green of a corpse. Its rider is named Death, and Hades follows. The colour itself signals death and disease.

meanings.note: Death kills by sword, famine, pestilence and wild beasts, echoing Ezekiel's four judgements.
Authority is 'given' over a quarter of the earth: the judgement is real but bounded by God.

meanings.meaning: Terror and sickness on the face
meanings.note: Hebrew speaks of faces turning pale or greenish (yeraqon) in terror.

otUsage: Faces turning pale with fear (Jer 30:6); horses of different colours patrolling the earth in Zechariah (Zech 1:8; Zech 6:2-3), the background for Revelation's four horses.
ntUsage: Only Rev 6:8 as a horse colour; chlōros elsewhere means green (Mark 6:39; Rev 8:7; Rev 9:4).
caution: Linking the pale horse to a particular modern pandemic or to Islam (because of green flags) is speculative. Revelation's horsemen describe recurring realities of war, famine and death.

name: Lamb
original: Hebrew seh, kebes; Greek amnos, arnion
plain: Lambs were the common sacrifice in Israel, above all at Passover. John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world', and Revelation's central figure is a Lamb standing as though slain, who is also the conquering ruler.

meanings.meaning: The Passover lamb and rescue from death
meanings.note: The lamb's blood marked the houses spared. John notes Jesus' bones were not broken, like the Passover lamb; Paul calls Christ 'our Passover'.

meanings.meaning: The suffering servant led to slaughter
meanings.note: Philip applies Isa 53 to Jesus. 'A lamb without blemish' combines the sacrificial requirement with sinlessness.

Abraham's words on Moriah are widely read by Christians as pointing to Christ. Jewish tradition reflects deeply on Isaac's binding (the Aqedah). The link to John 1:29 is a common typology, not stated in John.

meanings.meaning: Which lamb is the 'Lamb of God'?
meanings.note: Scholars debate whether John means the Passover lamb, the servant of Isa 53, the daily temple lamb (tamid), the lamb of Gen 22, or a warrior-lamb of Jewish apocalyptic (as in *1 Enoch* 89-90). Many think several are combined.
John hears of a Lion and sees a Lamb (Rev 5:5-6): Christ conquers by self-giving death. The Lamb is worshipped, shepherds, judges, marries his bride and lights the city.

otUsage: Abel's offering of the flock (Gen 4:4), Passover (Exod 12), daily morning and evening lambs (Num 28:3-4), the servant as a lamb (Isa 53:7), the wolf lying with the lamb (Isa 11:6; Isa 65:25).
ntUsage: John the Baptist's witness (John 1:29), Philip and the eunuch (Acts 8:32), Christ our Passover (1 Cor 5:7), the blameless lamb (1 Pet 1:19), and nearly thirty times in Revelation (arnion). Disciples as lambs among wolves (Luke 10:3) and Jesus' 'feed my lambs' (John 21:15).
caution: Revelation's beast from the earth has 'two horns like a lamb' (Rev 13:11): a lamb-like look is no guarantee of truth. Passover was not formally a sin offering, so the NT's lamb imagery blends several sacrifices rather than mapping one-to-one.

name: Lion
original: Hebrew ari, aryeh, kephir, labi; Greek leōn
plain: Lions lived in ancient Israel and were the most feared predator. The lion stands for royal strength (the Lion of Judah), for God's roaring judgement, and also for deadly enemies, including the devil 'like a roaring lion'. The same animal can picture God or his enemies.

meanings.meaning: Royal power of Judah and the Messiah
meanings.note: Jacob's blessing calls Judah a lion's cub with the sceptre. Revelation names Jesus 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah'.
'The lion has roared; who will not fear?' God is like a lion against his unfaithful people, and also roars to gather them home.
Persecutors and Satan are lions that devour. Paul was 'rescued from the lion's mouth', probably meaning a lethal danger rather than literal lions.
'The righteous are bold as a lion.'

meanings.meaning: A face of the throne creatures and a Gospel symbol
meanings.note: One of the four faces. Later tradition linked the lion to Mark (Jerome) or to John (Irenaeus); tradition varies.

otUsage: Samson and David kill lions (Judg 14:5-6; 1 Sam 17:34-37), a disobedient prophet killed by a lion (1 Kgs 13:24), Daniel in the den (Dan 6:22), Babylon as a winged lion (Dan 7:4), the lion eating straw in the peaceable kingdom (Isa 11:7).
ntUsage: The devil as a roaring lion (1 Pet 5:8), the faithful who shut lions' mouths (Heb 11:33), the Lion of Judah (Rev 5:5), a lion-like beast (Rev 13:2).
caution: C. S. Lewis's Aslan has made the lion a popular Christ image; that is a modern literary use. In Scripture the lion is morally neutral, and context decides.

name: Dove
original: Hebrew yonah, tor (turtledove); Greek peristera, trygōn
plain: Doves were gentle, common birds and the poor family's sacrifice. A dove brought Noah the olive leaf, and the Spirit descended on Jesus 'like a dove' at his baptism. Doves also picture innocence, love, mourning and, in Hosea, silliness.

meanings.note: All four Gospels use the image; Luke says 'in bodily form like a dove'. Some link it to the Spirit hovering over the waters (Gen 1:2), which rabbinic tradition likened to a hovering dove (Talmud *Hagigah* 15a). That connection is tradition.

meanings.meaning: New creation and peace after judgement
meanings.note: The dove finds no rest, then returns with an olive leaf. The modern peace symbol of dove and olive branch grew from this story.
Mary and Joseph offer the poor family's sacrifice. Temple dove-sellers were driven out by Jesus (Matt 21:12).
'Wise as serpents, innocent as doves.' The beloved is 'my dove'.
Ephraim is a silly dove flitting between Egypt and Assyria; doves' cooing sounds like moaning.

otUsage: Noah's dove (Gen 8:8-12), Abraham's covenant offering (Gen 15:9), poor offerings (Lev 12:8), longing for dove's wings (Ps 55:6), Jonah's name means dove (Jonah 1:1), exiles returning like doves (Hos 11:11).
ntUsage: Jesus' baptism (Matt 3:16), sacrifice for Jesus' presentation (Luke 2:24), temple sellers (John 2:14), innocence (Matt 10:16).
caution: Some preachers make Jonah ('dove') a type of the Spirit or of Israel; that is a name-based link with little textual support.

name: Serpent
original: Hebrew nachash, saraph, tannin; Greek ophis, drakōn
plain: The serpent in Eden deceives Eve and is cursed, and Revelation names 'that ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan'. Yet the same image is used for healing: the bronze serpent Moses lifted up, which Jesus compares to his own lifting up on the cross.

meanings.meaning: Deceiver and enemy of God's people
meanings.note: Genesis does not name the serpent as Satan; later Jewish writing (*Wisdom of Solomon* 2:24) and the NT make that identification. Gen 3:15 has been read since Irenaeus as the first gospel promise (the 'protoevangelium'); many modern scholars read it more generally as lasting conflict between humans and evil.

meanings.meaning: Healing through what was lifted up
meanings.note: Looking at the bronze serpent healed the bitten. Jesus uses it of his crucifixion.

meanings.meaning: An object that became an idol
meanings.note: Hezekiah smashed the bronze serpent (called Nehushtan) because people burned incense to it. Good symbols can become idols.
The serpent was 'crafty' (Hebrew arum, a pun on 'naked', arummim, in Gen 2:25). Jesus tells disciples to be wise as serpents, without guile.
Disciples tread on serpents; Paul shakes off a viper. Mark 16:18 also mentions handling snakes, but that is in the longer ending of Mark, missing from the earliest manuscripts.

otUsage: Eden (Gen 3), Moses' staff turned to a snake (Exod 4:3; Exod 7:10-12), fiery serpents (Num 21:6), wine biting like a serpent (Prov 23:32), Leviathan the twisting serpent (Isa 27:1), the serpent eating dust in the new creation (Isa 65:25).
ntUsage: Brood of vipers (Matt 3:7; Matt 23:33), bread or a snake (Matt 7:10), the lifted serpent (John 3:14), Paul's viper (Acts 28:3), the ancient serpent (Rev 12:9).
caution: The fiery serpents (seraphim) of Num 21:6 share a word with the seraphim of Isa 6:2; some scholars think the seraphim were pictured as winged serpents, others disagree. Snake-handling as a test of faith rests on a textually uncertain verse.

name: Eagle (and vulture)
plain: The eagle in the Bible is a symbol of strength, speed, care and renewal, especially in 'they shall mount up with wings as eagles'. The Hebrew word nesher often means the griffon vulture, so some passages that say 'eagle' picture birds gathering at carcasses.

meanings.note: God bore Israel 'on eagles' wings', like a bird stirring and carrying its young.
Those who wait on the LORD rise up with fresh strength.

meanings.meaning: Swift invading armies and proud kingdoms
meanings.note: Babylon is a great eagle; Edom nests among the stars but will be brought down.
Many translations now say 'vultures'. Jesus' saying means judgement will be as obvious as birds circling a body. A Roman-eagle reading (the legions' standards) is sometimes proposed; it is debated.

meanings.meaning: A face of the throne creatures and a Gospel symbol
meanings.note: The woman of Rev 12 receives eagle's wings to flee to the wilderness, echoing the exodus. Church tradition (Jerome, Augustine) assigned the eagle to John's soaring Gospel.

otUsage: Unclean bird (Lev 11:13), the exodus image (Exod 19:4), Saul and Jonathan swifter than eagles (2 Sam 1:23), Babylon as an eagle (Ezek 17:3), winged lion (Dan 7:4).
ntUsage: Vultures at the carcass (Matt 24:28), the fourth living creature (Rev 4:7), an eagle crying woe (Rev 8:13), eagle's wings for the woman (Rev 12:14).
caution: The legend that the eagle renews youth by flying near the sun and plunging into water comes from medieval bestiaries, not from Ps 103:5.

name: Ox, bull and calf
original: Hebrew shor, par, egel, baqar; Greek bous, moschos, tauros
plain: Oxen were the farmer's strength, pulling ploughs and carts, and bulls were the most costly sacrifice. The ox stands for labour and strength, the bull for sacrifice and for power that could become an idol, as with the golden calf.

meanings.note: 'Do not muzzle the ox while it treads grain.' Paul applies it to paying gospel workers.
Bulls were offered for the priest's sin and on the Day of Atonement; Hebrews contrasts them with Christ's self-offering.
The golden calf and Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan. Bulls were common symbols for gods like Baal; some scholars think the calves were pedestals for an invisible God rather than images of him.

meanings.meaning: A face of the throne creatures and a Gospel symbol
meanings.note: Tradition linked the ox (or calf) with Luke, whose Gospel begins with a priest offering in the temple.
'The ox knows its owner, but Israel does not know.' This verse later inspired the ox and donkey in nativity scenes.

otUsage: Goring ox laws (Exod 21:28), twelve bronze oxen under the sea (1 Kgs 7:25), Elisha ploughing with twelve yoke (1 Kgs 19:19), lion eating straw like the ox (Isa 11:7).
ntUsage: Rescuing an ox on the sabbath (Luke 14:5), the fatted calf (Luke 15:23), the yoke (Matt 11:29-30), muzzled ox (1 Cor 9:9), calf-faced creature (Rev 4:7).
caution: The law not to plough with ox and donkey together (Deut 22:10) is often linked to 'unequally yoked' (2 Cor 6:14); Paul does not cite it, so the link is a likely echo at best.

name: Horse
plain: In Bible times horses were war machines, not farm animals. They stand for military might, which Israel was warned not to trust. In visions, coloured horses carry God's judgements through the earth, and Christ returns on a white horse.

meanings.note: 'Some trust in chariots and some in horses.' Kings were not to multiply horses.
Chariots and horses of fire surround Elisha.

meanings.meaning: Agents of judgement through the earth
meanings.note: Revelation's four horsemen draw on Zechariah. The first rider on a white horse is debated: Christ or the gospel's advance (some Fathers), or a conqueror and false messiah who imitates Christ (many modern readers).
The rider called Faithful and True, the Word of God, wins with the sword from his mouth.
Bit and bridle picture discipline of speech and stubbornness.

otUsage: Pharaoh's horses in the sea (Exod 15:1), Solomon's horse trade (1 Kgs 10:28), the warhorse of Job (Job 39:19-25), renouncing horses (Hos 14:3), the king who cuts off the war-horse (Zech 9:10).
ntUsage: Bits in horses' mouths (Jas 3:3), the horsemen (Rev 6), demonic cavalry (Rev 9:16-17), the white horse of Christ (Rev 19:11).
caution: The contrast between horse and donkey matters: the messianic king of Zech 9:9-10 rides a donkey and removes the war-horse.

name: Donkey
original: Hebrew chamor, aton (she-donkey), ayir (colt); Greek onos, pōlos
plain: Donkeys were the everyday working animal and could also be the mount of leaders in peacetime. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah's picture of a king who comes humbly and brings peace. Balaam's donkey famously sees the angel and speaks.

meanings.note: Matthew has a donkey and a colt; many take this as reading Zechariah's poetic parallel literally, others think two animals were really present. Either way the king comes in peace, not on a war-horse.
Leaders rode donkeys; Solomon was crowned on David's mule. So the donkey is humble compared to a war-horse, but not shameful.
Balaam's donkey sees the angel the prophet cannot see.
Binding a donkey to a vine pictures such plenty that no one minds the donkey eating the grapes. Many read it as messianic, echoed in Zech 9:9.

otUsage: Abraham's donkey to Moriah (Gen 22:3), firstborn donkeys redeemed with a lamb (Exod 13:13), Saul looking for lost donkeys (1 Sam 9:3), Samson's jawbone (Judg 15:15), the burial of a donkey as disgrace (Jer 22:19).
ntUsage: Triumphal entry (Matt 21:5), untying a donkey on the sabbath (Luke 13:15), Balaam's donkey (2 Pet 2:16). The donkey at the nativity is tradition (from Isa 1:3), not in the Gospels.
caution: The ancient slur that Jews or Christians worshipped a donkey (reported by Tertullian and seen in the Alexamenos graffito) is a pagan insult, not a biblical symbol.

name: Sheep and shepherd
original: Hebrew tson, roeh (shepherd); Greek probaton, poimēn
plain: Israel was a nation of shepherds, so God's people are pictured as sheep and their leaders as shepherds. God is the true shepherd, bad kings are condemned as false shepherds, and Jesus calls himself the Good Shepherd who lays down his life.

meanings.note: Kings across the ancient Near East were called shepherds; Israel applies the title first to God.

meanings.meaning: Leaders as shepherds, good and bad
meanings.note: Leaders who feed themselves instead of the flock are judged. Elders are told to shepherd willingly. 'Pastor' comes from the Latin for shepherd.
Jesus claims the role God promised for himself and for a coming David. He knows, calls, gathers and dies for the sheep.

meanings.meaning: People who are lost or helpless
meanings.note: Sheep without a shepherd wander and scatter.

meanings.meaning: Sheep and goats at the judgement
meanings.note: Shepherds separated mixed flocks at night. See 'goat' for the point and its limits.

otUsage: Abel, the patriarchs, Moses and David as shepherds (Gen 4:2; Exod 3:1; 1 Sam 16:11), the struck shepherd and scattered sheep (Zech 13:7), the coming ruler who shepherds (Mic 5:4).
ntUsage: Shepherds at the nativity (Luke 2:8), the lost sheep (Luke 15:4), the Good Shepherd (John 10), 'feed my sheep' (John 21:17), the Lamb who shepherds (Rev 7:17).
caution: Sheep imagery is about dependence on a good shepherd, not a call to unthinking passivity; the same texts judge abusive leaders harshly.

name: Goat
original: Hebrew ez, sair, attud; Greek eriphos, tragos
plain: Goats were ordinary flock animals and acceptable sacrifices. On the Day of Atonement one goat was sacrificed and another, the scapegoat, carried Israel's sins into the wilderness. In Jesus' parable, goats on the left stand for those who failed to care for 'the least of these'.

meanings.note: One goat is 'for the LORD', the other 'for Azazel'. Azazel is debated: a wilderness demon, a place name, or 'the goat that goes away'. Christians see both goats fulfilled in Christ's death and removal of sin.
Male goats were regular sin offerings; Hebrews says such blood cannot finally remove sin.
The sheep and goats are judged by how they treated Christ's 'least' brothers and sisters. Who the 'least' are (all needy people or Christian messengers) is debated.
The he-goat is the king of Greece, generally identified with Alexander the Great.
Jacob deceives Isaac with goat-skins; years later his sons deceive him with a goat's blood on Joseph's coat.

otUsage: Passover could be a lamb or goat (Exod 12:5), goat-hair curtains (Exod 26:7), goat-demons or 'satyrs' (Lev 17:7; Isa 13:21), the beloved's hair like goats (Song 4:1), Ezekiel judging between rams and goats (Ezek 34:17).
ntUsage: Sheep and goats (Matt 25:32), the older brother's complaint about never getting a goat (Luke 15:29), blood of goats (Heb 9:12).
caution: Goats are not inherently evil; they were clean animals and valid sacrifices. The modern devil-with-goat-horns imagery comes from later art, not from Scripture.

name: Wolf
plain: The wolf is the enemy of the flock. Scripture uses it for violent rulers, false teachers who come 'in sheep's clothing', and the dangers disciples face. In the age to come, the wolf will live peacefully with the lamb.

meanings.note: Wolves in sheep's clothing; savage wolves entering the flock; officials like wolves tearing prey.

meanings.meaning: A hostile world for the disciples
meanings.note: Disciples are sent as sheep among wolves; the hired hand flees when the wolf comes.
Whether this is literal peace among animals or a picture of peace between enemies (or both) is debated.
Benjamin is 'a ravenous wolf', a warrior tribe. Some Fathers applied it to Paul, a Benjaminite who once 'ravaged' the church (Phil 3:5); tradition.

otUsage: Benjamin (Gen 49:27), wolves of the evening (Hab 1:8; Zeph 3:3), a wolf destroying the disobedient (Jer 5:6), the wolf with the lamb (Isa 11:6).
ntUsage: False prophets (Matt 7:15), sheep among wolves (Luke 10:3), the hireling and the wolf (John 10:12), Paul's warning to Ephesian elders (Acts 20:29).
caution: 'Wolf' was used for real dangers; using it to dismiss anyone who disagrees with us turns a warning into a weapon.

name: Dog
original: Hebrew kelev; Greek kyōn, kynarion (little dog)
plain: In the Bible most dogs were half-wild scavengers, not pets, so 'dog' was usually an insult for someone contemptible, unclean or dangerous. Yet the Canaanite woman turns Jesus' 'little dogs' saying into a plea of faith.

meanings.note: 'Am I a dog?' 'A dead dog' was a strong phrase of self-abasement or insult.

meanings.meaning: Scavengers as a sign of judgement
meanings.note: Being eaten by dogs was the worst dishonour. In Ps 22 enemies surround like dogs.
A dog returning to its vomit pictures people going back to what harmed them.

meanings.meaning: Outsiders, and how they receive grace
meanings.note: Jewish speech sometimes called Gentiles dogs. Jesus' 'little dogs' saying and the woman's reply lead to praise of her faith. Readers debate whether Jesus was testing her, voicing a common view to overturn it, or genuinely persuaded.

meanings.meaning: Those excluded from the holy city
meanings.note: Paul turns the insult on Christian circumcision-teachers. In Deut 23:18 'dog' may refer to a male cult prostitute; the meaning is debated.

otUsage: Not a dog moving its tongue at the exodus (Exod 11:7), unclean meat thrown to dogs (Exod 22:31), Gideon's men lapping like dogs (Judg 7:5), silent watchdogs as lazy prophets (Isa 56:10), a living dog better than a dead lion (Eccl 9:4).
ntUsage: Do not give what is holy to dogs (Matt 7:6), dogs licking Lazarus' sores (Luke 16:21), the Canaanite woman (Matt 15:27), 'beware of dogs' (Phil 3:2), outside the city (Rev 22:15).
caution: A friendly dog appears in the deuterocanonical book of Tobit, travelling with Tobias. The Bible's negative uses reflect street dogs of the time, not a judgement on dogs today.

name: Pig (swine)
plain: Pigs were unclean under the law of Moses, so they became a symbol of what is unclean or of the far, Gentile world. In Jesus' teaching, the prodigal son feeding pigs has hit bottom, and the demons sent into a herd of pigs show that 'Legion' is defeated.

meanings.note: Eating pork marked rebellion in Isaiah. Under the Seleucids, Jews were pressured to eat pork and some died refusing (told in 2 Maccabees 6-7).
A Jewish son feeding a Gentile's pigs, longing for their food, has lost everything.

meanings.meaning: Unable to value what is holy
meanings.note: Pearls before swine; a gold ring in a pig's snout.

Unclean spirits go into unclean animals in Gentile territory and are drowned. Some scholars note the boar was the emblem of the Roman Tenth Legion stationed in the region and see a jab at Rome in 'Legion'; that is speculative.

Mark comments that Jesus 'declared all foods clean'; Peter's vision includes unclean animals. Christians debate how and when food laws ceased to apply, but most agree they do not bind Gentile believers.

otUsage: Food laws (Lev 11:7), the wild boar ravaging God's vine (Ps 80:13), pig's blood in idolatrous worship (Isa 66:3).
ntUsage: Pearls before swine (Matt 7:6), the Gerasene pigs (Mark 5:13), the prodigal (Luke 15:15), the washed pig back in the mud (2 Pet 2:22).
caution: The point of the pig is ritual status, not hygiene. The 'health reasons' explanation for food laws is a modern idea that the text does not give.

name: Raven
plain: Ravens were unclean scavengers, yet God feeds them and uses them to feed Elijah. Jesus points to the ravens to show that God cares for those who seem least deserving, so his people need not worry.

meanings.note: Jesus: they neither sow nor reap, yet God feeds them. How much more you.
Unclean birds bring bread and meat to the prophet. A few scholars repoint the Hebrew to read 'Arabians' instead of 'ravens'; most keep ravens.
The raven goes to and fro and does not return, unlike the dove. Fathers sometimes read the raven as the unclean or unrepentant; tradition.
Ravens inhabit ruins and peck out the eyes of the scornful.

otUsage: Unclean bird (Lev 11:15; Deut 14:14), Noah's raven (Gen 8:7), Elijah's ravens (1 Kgs 17:6), ravens in ruined Edom (Isa 34:11), hair black as a raven (Song 5:11).
ntUsage: Only Luke 12:24 (Matthew says 'birds of the air', Matt 6:26).
caution: That ravens are unclean sharpens the point of providence; it does not make them symbols of evil in every text.

name: Fish
plain: Fish were a staple food around Galilee, and several disciples were fishermen. Jesus calls them to 'fish for people', multiplies fish, and eats fish after rising. Early Christians used the Greek word for fish, ICHTHYS, as an acrostic for 'Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour'.

meanings.note: In Jeremiah fishers gather for judgement; Jesus turns the image toward gathering people into the kingdom.
A dragnet gathers every kind; good and bad are separated at the end.
Feeding the crowds; breakfast on the shore; Ezekiel's river makes the Dead Sea teem with fish.
Jesus eats fish to show he is not a ghost.

The letters stand for Iesous Christos Theou Yios Soter. Tertullian (*On Baptism* 1) calls Christians little fish after the great Fish, and Augustine (*City of God* 18.23) discusses the acrostic. This is early church tradition, not biblical symbolism.

otUsage: Creation of sea creatures (Gen 1:21), the great fish of Jonah (Jonah 1:17), clean and unclean fish (Lev 11:9-12), fish dying in the Nile plague (Exod 7:21), people caught like fish (Hab 1:14-15; Eccl 9:12).
ntUsage: Fishermen disciples (Mark 1:16-17), feedings (Mark 6:41), the coin in the fish (Matt 17:27), the sign of Jonah (Matt 12:40), 153 fish (John 21:11).
caution: The idea that 'the sign of the fish' was a secret code drawn in the sand during persecution is a popular story with little ancient evidence. The Philistine god Dagon is often said to be a fish-god, but most scholars now link the name to grain.

name: Locust
original: Hebrew arbeh (and other words); Greek akris
plain: Locust swarms could strip a land bare, so they were a terrifying image of judgement and invading armies. Yet locusts were also clean food: John the Baptist ate locusts and wild honey. Revelation's locusts from the abyss are demonic and nightmarish.

meanings.note: The eighth plague; covenant curse; Solomon's prayer for relief.
Joel's locusts are either a real plague described as an army, a real army described as locusts, or both stages. Scholars debate.
'I will restore the years the locust has eaten.'
Locusts with human faces and scorpion tails, led by Abaddon/Apollyon. Modern attempts to identify them as helicopters or aircraft are speculative.
Most scholars take these as insects (permitted food). The 'locust bean' or carob pod reading is a later suggestion.

otUsage: Plague in Egypt (Exod 10), clean insects (Lev 11:22), spies 'like grasshoppers' (Num 13:33), Midianite hordes (Judg 6:5), Amos' vision (Amos 7:1), locusts with no king who still march in ranks (Prov 30:27).
ntUsage: John's diet (Matt 3:4; Mark 1:6) and the fifth trumpet (Rev 9:3-11).
caution: Locusts are a vivid image, but not every swarm or pest outbreak today is a 'sign'. Context in Joel and Revelation is judgement calling for repentance.

name: Leviathan
plain: Leviathan is a great sea creature in Hebrew poetry. Sometimes it seems to be a real animal (a crocodile or whale) that only God can tame; sometimes it is a many-headed chaos monster that God crushes. Either way the point is God's total mastery over the most frightening powers.

meanings.meaning: A creature only God can master
meanings.note: In Job, God asks if Job can catch Leviathan with a hook. Many identify it with the crocodile; others see a mythic beast described with real animal features. In Ps 104 it is God's creature playing in the sea.

meanings.meaning: Chaos and evil defeated by God
meanings.note: God crushed Leviathan's heads; he will slay 'Leviathan the twisting serpent'. Texts from Ugarit describe a seven-headed sea serpent called Litan with very similar wording, so Israel used a known image to declare that the LORD, not Baal, rules the sea.
In Ps 74 crushing Leviathan is linked to the Red Sea; Egypt is elsewhere a sea-dragon.

meanings.meaning: Background to Revelation's dragon and sea beast
meanings.note: The many-headed dragon and the beast from the sea draw on this imagery. The term Leviathan itself is not used in the NT.

ntUsage: Not named; its imagery informs the dragon and sea beast of Revelation (Rev 12-13). Rev 21:1 'no more sea' completes the defeat of chaos.
caution: Reading Leviathan as a surviving dinosaur or sea reptile is a modern young-earth creationist proposal and is not the scholarly consensus. Later Jewish writings (2 Baruch, rabbinic texts) imagined Leviathan served at the messianic banquet; that is tradition.

name: Behemoth
plain: Behemoth appears in God's speech to Job as a massive land creature, 'the first of the works of God', that only its Maker can approach with a sword. The name means something like 'the Beast' or 'the super-beast'. Most identify it with the hippopotamus; others see a mythic creature.

meanings.note: God shows Job a creature far beyond human control to humble him and to show God's wise rule even over the wild.

meanings.meaning: Identity: hippopotamus, elephant, or mythic beast
meanings.note: It lies under lotus plants in the reeds and is unafraid of a raging river, which fits the hippo. 'Tail like a cedar' (Job 40:17) is hard for the hippo; some read 'tail' as a euphemism, others as poetic exaggeration. Later Jewish texts (*1 Enoch* 60:7-8) pair a land-monster Behemoth with sea-monster Leviathan.
Some young-earth creationists identify Behemoth with a sauropod because of the 'tail like a cedar'. Most biblical scholars do not accept this.

otUsage: Only Job 40:15-24 as a proper name; the ordinary plural 'beasts' (behemot) appears often, as in Ps 73:22 ('I was a beast before you').
ntUsage: Not used.
caution: Job's point is not zoology. The creature humbles human pride and shows God's sovereign care over things that terrify us.

name: Dragon (sea monster)
plain: The Hebrew tannin can mean a large sea creature, a snake or a sea monster. In poetry it stands for chaos and for proud empires like Egypt and Babylon. In Revelation the great red dragon is Satan, who wars against the woman and her child and gives power to the beast.

meanings.note: The dragon is explicitly identified as 'that ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan'. Seven heads and ten horns link him to the beasts he empowers.
Pharaoh is the great dragon in the Nile; Nebuchadnezzar swallowed Judah like a dragon. Rahab here is a sea-monster name, not Rahab of Jericho.
God created the great tanninim; they praise him. Even the monsters are creatures.
The LORD slays the dragon in the sea; the faithful trample it.

otUsage: Sea creatures (Gen 1:21), Aaron's staff becomes a tannin (Exod 7:9-10), venom of dragons (Deut 32:33), Egypt and Babylon (Ezek 29:3; Jer 51:34).
ntUsage: Only Revelation: the red dragon (Rev 12:3), its gift of power to the beast (Rev 13:2-4), frog-like spirits from its mouth (Rev 16:13), bound for a thousand years (Rev 20:2).
caution: The KJV uses 'dragons' for jackals in several prophets (e.g. Isa 13:22; Jer 9:11; Mic 1:8) by confusing two similar Hebrew words (tan, jackal; tannin, sea monster). Modern versions correct this. 'Bel and the Dragon' is an addition to Daniel in the deuterocanon.

name: The beast (Daniel 7 and Revelation 13)
plain: In Daniel 7 four monstrous beasts rise from the sea and stand for world empires, until 'one like a son of man' receives the kingdom. Revelation 13 combines their features into one beast from the sea, aided by a second beast from the land. The beast is political power that demands worship. Who it refers to has been one of the most debated questions in Christian history.

meanings.note: The angel explains the beasts as kings or kingdoms. Traditional reading: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome. Most critical scholars: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece (ending with Antiochus IV as the little horn). Both views have able defenders.

meanings.meaning: Beastly power versus the human Son of Man
meanings.note: Empires are beasts; God's kingdom is given to a human figure and to the saints. Jesus applies the Son of Man to himself.

Seven hills and seven kings fit Rome. The healed death-wound may echo the legend that Nero would return (reported by Tacitus and Suetonius). Widely held by modern scholars as at least the first reference.
A final world ruler before Christ returns. Held by many evangelicals and dispensationalists; also by some early Fathers.

meanings.meaning: The papacy, or recurring tyranny (historicist and idealist readings)
meanings.note: Many Reformers identified the beast or Antichrist with the papacy; this view has largely faded and is rejected by Catholics. Idealists see a pattern repeating in every age when the state claims divine honours.

otUsage: Daniel's four beasts (Dan 7), ram and goat (Dan 8:20-21), with background in the sea monster imagery of Leviathan.
ntUsage: Revelation's sea beast and land beast or false prophet (Rev 13:1; Rev 13:11; Rev 16:13), the beast from the abyss (Rev 11:7; Rev 17:8), its defeat (Rev 19:20; Rev 20:10).
caution: Each generation has found 'the beast' in its own enemies. A wise reading notices what the beast does (deceives, demands worship, persecutes, controls trade) and resists those patterns, rather than confidently naming one person.

name: Vine and vineyard
original: Hebrew gefen, kerem (vineyard); Greek ampelos, ampelōn
plain: The grapevine was one of Israel's main crops, so Israel itself is pictured as God's vine or vineyard, which he planted and tended but which gave bad fruit. Jesus says, 'I am the true vine'; his followers live by staying joined to him. Sitting under one's own vine pictures peace and security.

meanings.note: God brought a vine out of Egypt; he looked for good grapes and found wild ones.

Jesus takes Israel's identity on himself: as the faithful vine he gives life to branches who abide in him. Whether 'taken away' branches (John 15:2) are lost believers or never-true disciples is debated.
The parable of the tenants reuses Isaiah's vineyard song against the leaders of Jesus' day.
'Everyone under his vine and fig tree, with none to make them afraid.'

meanings.meaning: The fruit of the vine and the kingdom feast
meanings.note: Wine looks ahead to the messianic banquet. Herod's temple had a great golden vine over its entrance (described by Josephus), so the image was very public.

otUsage: Noah's vineyard (Gen 9:20), the cupbearer's dream (Gen 40:9-11), spies' huge cluster (Num 13:23), Jotham's fable (Judg 9:12-13), Naboth's vineyard (1 Kgs 21:1), useless vine wood (Ezek 15:2-6), vine of Sodom (Deut 32:32).
ntUsage: Labourers in the vineyard (Matt 20:1-16), wicked tenants (Mark 12:1-9), the barren fig in a vineyard (Luke 13:6), the true vine (John 15:1), the grape harvest of judgement (Rev 14:18-20).
caution: Vine imagery can be comforting (abiding) and severe (pruning, burning). Reading only one side distorts it.

name: Fig tree
plain: Figs were a staple fruit, and the fig tree stood for peace and prosperity, and for Israel's fruitfulness or lack of it. Jesus' cursing of a fruitless fig tree, wrapped around his action in the temple, is widely read as an acted warning against the temple establishment.

meanings.note: Sitting under vine and fig tree.
God found Israel like early figs; Jeremiah's good and bad figs; Jesus' parable of the barren fig tree given one more year.
Mark sandwiches the temple clearing between the cursing and the withered tree. Most scholars read it as an enacted parable about the temple; Jesus also draws a lesson on faith and prayer.

When the fig tree puts out leaves, summer is near. The popular claim that the fig tree is modern Israel and its 'budding' was 1948 is a speculative dispensational reading; Luke says 'the fig tree and all the trees'.
Jesus' knowledge amazes Nathanael. Some suggest he was studying Scripture there, as later rabbis spoke of studying under fig trees; this is speculative.

otUsage: Fig leaves in Eden (Gen 3:7), the fig tree declining kingship in Jotham's fable (Judg 9:10-11), a fig poultice for Hezekiah (Isa 38:21), loss of figs in judgement (Joel 1:7; Hab 3:17).
ntUsage: Fruit by its tree (Jas 3:12), the cursed fig (Mark 11:13), the parable (Luke 13:6), lesson of the fig (Matt 24:32), stars falling like unripe figs (Rev 6:13).
caution: Mark notes 'it was not the season for figs' (Mark 11:13). This is part of what makes the act symbolic; it is not best read as an outburst of temper.

name: Olive tree and olive oil
original: Hebrew zayit, shemen (oil); Greek elaia, elaion
plain: The long-lived olive tree gave oil for food, light, medicine and anointing kings and priests. It stands for God's blessing, for Israel, and for the Spirit-anointed. Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive branches grafted into Israel's tree.

meanings.note: 'Messiah' (Hebrew mashiach) and 'Christ' (Greek christos) both mean 'anointed one', anointed with olive oil.
Paul's point is humility: the root supports the branches. How this relates to the future of ethnic Israel is debated (see the Israel-and-church debate).
A green olive in God's house; children like olive shoots; the olive leaf after the flood.

meanings.meaning: The two olive trees: anointed witnesses
meanings.note: In Zechariah, probably Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the priest. In Revelation, the two witnesses, read as the church's prophetic witness, as two end-time prophets, or as figures like Moses and Elijah.
Oil for the lamp, for wounds and for prayer over the sick. Oil as a symbol of the Holy Spirit is a common Christian reading drawn from anointing; it is not stated directly.

otUsage: Promised land of olive oil (Deut 8:8), Jotham's fable (Judg 9:8-9), cherubim of olive wood in the temple (1 Kgs 6:23), gleanings left for the poor (Deut 24:20; Isa 17:6), the Mount of Olives (Zech 14:4).
ntUsage: Gethsemane, whose name means 'oil press' (Matt 26:36), the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39; Acts 1:12), the good Samaritan's oil (Luke 10:34), the olive tree in Romans 11, two olive trees (Rev 11:4).
caution: The image of Jesus being 'pressed like olives' in Gethsemane is a devotional reflection on the name, not something the Gospels themselves draw out.

name: Cedar of Lebanon
plain: The tall, fragrant, rot-resistant cedars of Lebanon were the finest building timber in the ancient Near East. Cedar stands for strength, majesty and pride: used for God's temple, a picture of the flourishing righteous, and an image of arrogant empires that God cuts down.

meanings.note: David lives in a house of cedar while the ark is in a tent; Solomon's temple is lined with cedar.
'The righteous shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.'
Assyria is a towering cedar felled. God's voice breaks the cedars.
God takes a tender shoot from the top of the cedar and plants it on a high mountain, and birds nest in it. Many scholars see this behind Jesus' mustard-seed parable.
Cedar wood, scarlet and hyssop were used together in purification. Perhaps chosen for durability or fragrance; the reason is not stated.

otUsage: Temple and palace building (1 Kgs 7:2), Jotham's fable (Judg 9:15), Jehoash's fable of thistle and cedar (2 Kgs 14:9), Solomon's botany from cedar to hyssop (1 Kgs 4:33), Jehoiakim's cedar palace condemned (Jer 22:14-15).
ntUsage: Not mentioned by name in the NT; its imagery of birds nesting in a great tree echoes in the mustard-seed parable (Mark 4:32).
caution: Cedar's meaning flips between noble and arrogant. Read the context.

name: Mustard seed
