plain: Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a tiny mustard seed that grows into a large plant where birds nest, and says faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains. The point is small beginnings and surprising growth.

meanings.meaning: The kingdom's small start and great end
meanings.note: From a handful of Galilean disciples to a worldwide community.
Birds nesting in a great tree was a known image for peoples under a kingdom. Most read the birds as nations, including Gentiles, coming into God's kingdom.

Some interpreters (e.g. the *Scofield Reference Bible*) note that birds in the sower parable are the evil one and read the mustard tree as Christendom grown unnaturally large and harbouring evil. A minority view.

meanings.meaning: Small faith in a great God
meanings.note: The power is in God, not the size of the faith.

otUsage: Mustard is not named in the OT. The great-tree-with-birds image comes from Ezek 17:22-23, Ezek 31:6 and Dan 4:10-12.
ntUsage: The parable (Mark 4:31), and faith like a mustard seed (Matt 17:20; Luke 17:6).
caution: 'Smallest of all seeds' is proverbial, not a botanical claim (orchid seeds are smaller). Mustard grows into a large shrub, not a true tree; Matthew and Luke's 'tree' may be a deliberate hint of Ezekiel's cedar, or a bit of humour about a humble garden plant.

name: Wheat and tares (weeds)
plain: Wheat was the staple grain, so it stands for true fruit and for God's people. In Jesus' parable an enemy sows weeds, almost certainly darnel, which looks like wheat until it heads. The farmer lets both grow until the harvest, when they are separated. Chaff, the husk blown away, is a picture of the worthless.

meanings.meaning: Good and evil growing together until the end
meanings.note: Jesus explains: the field is the world, the good seed the children of the kingdom, the weeds the children of the evil one, the harvest the end of the age.

Augustine used the parable against the Donatists to argue that the visible church contains both true and false members. Others note Jesus says the field is the world, not the church, and that discipline is still commanded. Debated.
The winnowing fork separates grain from chaff.
A grain of wheat must die to bear much fruit; Paul uses the seed for the resurrection body.
Satan asks to sift the disciples like wheat.

otUsage: Wheat harvest and the Feast of Weeks (Exod 34:22), land of wheat and barley (Deut 8:8), Ruth gleaning (Ruth 2:23), chaff driven by wind (Ps 1:4), sowing the wind (Hos 8:7).
ntUsage: Wheat and weeds (Matt 13:24-30), winnowing (Matt 3:12), the grain of wheat (John 12:24), sifting (Luke 22:31), the harvest of the earth (Rev 14:15-16).
caution: The parable warns against premature uprooting by human servants; it is not a denial that churches should exercise any discipline.

name: Thorns and thistles
original: Hebrew qots, dardar, shamir, seneh (thorn bush); Greek akantha, skolops
plain: Thorns come into the story with the curse on the ground after the fall. They picture frustration, judgement, worthless people and the cares that choke faith. At the cross, soldiers crown Jesus with thorns, and many Christians see him bearing the curse.

meanings.meaning: The curse on work and the ground
meanings.note: Isaiah promises that instead of the thorn will come up the cypress.

meanings.meaning: Crown of thorns: mock kingship and the curse borne
meanings.note: The soldiers mean mockery. Connecting the thorns to the curse of Gen 3 is an ancient Christian reflection, not stated in the Gospels.

meanings.meaning: Worries and riches that choke the word
meanings.note: In the sower parable.
Remaining Canaanites will be thorns in Israel's sides.
Greek skolops can mean a stake. Suggestions include poor eyesight, chronic illness, persecution, opponents (cf. Num 33:55) or temptation. No consensus.

otUsage: The curse (Gen 3:18), the burning bush, which was a thorn bush (Exod 3:2), Gideon's thorn-threshing (Judg 8:7), the bramble king (Judg 9:14-15), the vineyard overrun (Isa 5:6), thorns on the pagan altars (Hos 10:8).
ntUsage: Grapes not gathered from thorns (Matt 7:16), the sower (Matt 13:7), the crown (John 19:2), Paul's thorn (2 Cor 12:7), land bearing thorns (Heb 6:8).
caution: The ram 'caught in a thicket' (Gen 22:13) is sometimes linked to the crown of thorns. That is a devotional typology, not something the NT draws.

name: Hyssop
plain: Hyssop was a small, bushy herb (probably Syrian marjoram) used as a brush to sprinkle blood or water in rites of cleansing. It shows up at the first Passover, in David's prayer 'purge me with hyssop', and at the cross.

meanings.note: Hyssop dipped in the Passover lamb's blood marked the doorposts.
Used for cleansing skin disease, houses and corpse-impurity.
David asks for the purification only God can give.

Only John mentions hyssop (Mark and Matthew say 'a reed'). Many see a deliberate Passover link. A sprig of hyssop seems too weak to lift a sponge, so some have proposed a different Greek word (hyssos, javelin), found in one late manuscript. Debated.
Solomon's knowledge reached from the cedar to the hyssop on the wall, that is, from greatest to smallest.

otUsage: Passover (Exod 12:22), cleansing rites (Lev 14; Num 19), David's prayer (Ps 51:7), Solomon's botany (1 Kgs 4:33).
ntUsage: The cross (John 19:29) and Hebrews' summary of covenant sprinkling (Heb 9:19).
caution: The plant called hyssop today (Hyssopus officinalis) is probably not the biblical one.

name: Lily
plain: The biblical 'lily' is an unidentified bright flower, possibly the lotus, anemone or iris. It stands for beauty, love and God's lavish care. Jesus says to consider how the lilies grow: not even Solomon was dressed like one of them.

meanings.note: Wild flowers, here today and burned tomorrow, are dressed by God; how much more his children.
In Song 2:1 the woman most likely speaks ('I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys'). Applying it to Christ is a later devotional tradition.
'He shall blossom like the lily.'
Lily-work topped the pillars and the rim of the bronze sea, suggesting Eden-like beauty in God's house.
Medieval art made the white lily a sign of Mary's purity, and Easter lilies are a modern custom. Tradition, not biblical symbolism.

otUsage: Song of Songs (Song 2:1; Song 5:13), Hosea (Hos 14:5), temple pillars (1 Kgs 7:19), and psalm titles set 'to Lilies' (for example Ps 45 and Ps 69), probably a tune name.
ntUsage: Only in Jesus' saying about the lilies of the field (Matt 6:28; Luke 12:27).
caution: Exact flower identifications are uncertain. Do not build meaning on modern varieties like the white Easter lily.

name: Palm tree and palm branches
original: Hebrew tamar, kaf (palm frond); Greek phoinix
plain: The date palm was a tree of oases and abundance, and its branches were waved at festivals and victories. Crowds wave palm branches as Jesus enters Jerusalem, and the redeemed in Revelation hold palms before God's throne.

meanings.note: Palm branches were part of the booths and rejoicing at the Feast of Tabernacles.
Palms had been waved for the Maccabean liberators (1 and 2 Maccabees) and appeared on Jewish coins; the crowd hails Jesus as a national king. In Revelation they mark the victory of the redeemed.
'The righteous flourish like the palm tree.'
Carved palms with cherubim and flowers made the sanctuary a garden of God's presence.
Christian art gave martyrs the palm of victory, and the church remembers the triumphal entry on Palm Sunday. Tradition.

otUsage: Elim's seventy palms (Exod 15:27), Jericho the city of palms (Deut 34:3), Deborah judging under her palm (Judg 4:5), the name Tamar (Gen 38:6; 2 Sam 13:1), idols 'upright as the palm' (Jer 10:5).
ntUsage: Triumphal entry (John 12:13) and the great multitude (Rev 7:9).
caution: Only John mentions palms specifically at the entry; the other Gospels speak of branches and cloaks.

name: Almond (Aaron's rod)
plain: The almond is the first tree to blossom in Israel's late winter, so its Hebrew name shaqed sounds like 'the watcher' or 'wakeful one'. Aaron's dead staff budded, blossomed and bore almonds overnight to show God's choice of priest, and the tabernacle lampstand had almond-shaped cups.

meanings.note: Twelve staffs were laid before the LORD; only Aaron's came to life. It was kept before the ark as a sign against rebels.
A wordplay: Jeremiah sees an almond branch (shaqed) and God says he is watching (shoqed) to perform his word.

meanings.meaning: Light and life in the sanctuary
meanings.note: The lampstand's cups were shaped like almond blossoms, making it a stylised flowering tree. Many see an echo of the tree of life.
'The almond tree blossoms' probably pictures white hair. Debated but widely held.
Fathers saw the dead rod blooming as a figure of Christ's resurrection; others made it a type of the virgin birth (life from what could not naturally bear). Both are tradition.

otUsage: Gift of almonds to Joseph (Gen 43:11), Jacob's rods (Gen 30:37, where 'hazel' in KJV is probably almond, luz), the lampstand (Exod 25:33), Aaron's rod (Num 17:8), Jeremiah's vision (Jer 1:11), old age (Eccl 12:5).
ntUsage: Only Heb 9:4, listing Aaron's budded rod in the ark.
caution: Hebrew wordplay (shaqed and shoqed) is the key to Jeremiah 1; English readers can easily miss it and look for symbolism elsewhere.

name: Tree of life
original: Hebrew ets ha-chayyim; Greek xylon tēs zōēs
plain: The tree of life stood in the middle of Eden. After the fall, humans were barred from it. It returns at the end of the Bible, beside the river in the new Jerusalem, bearing fruit every month, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Between those, Proverbs uses it for wisdom and righteous living.

meanings.note: Barring the way can be read as judgement and as mercy (not living forever in a fallen state). Both readings appear in Jewish and Christian tradition.

meanings.meaning: Restored access in the new creation
meanings.note: The paradise of God is open again. Some manuscripts of Rev 22:19 read 'book of life' (KJV) instead of 'tree of life'; most modern texts read 'tree'.
Wisdom, the fruit of righteousness, fulfilled longing and gentle speech are each 'a tree of life'.

meanings.meaning: The cross as tree of life
meanings.note: The NT calls the cross a 'tree' (xylon). Early and medieval Christians linked it to the tree of life: the curse that came by a tree is undone by a tree. Tradition.

meanings.meaning: The lampstand as a stylised tree
meanings.note: Some scholars think the menorah, with branches and almond blossoms, recalls the tree of life in the sanctuary.

otUsage: Eden (Gen 2-3), Proverbs (Prov 3:18), the river of healing trees (Ezek 47:12), the righteous like a tree by streams (Ps 1:3).
ntUsage: Promise to the victorious at Ephesus (Rev 2:7) and the city's tree with twelve fruits (Rev 22:2).
caution: Kabbalah's 'tree of life' diagram is a much later mystical system and should not be read back into Genesis.
